newsitem.title: PAKISTAN: New Pakistan government sends mixed signals on IMF.
newsitem.headline: New Pakistan government sends mixed signals on IMF.

text.p: Pakistan's new government, apparently reluctant to swallow IMF medicine, nevertheless says that an IMF-agreed standby programme is still on the rails.
Abbas Mirakhor, who represents Pakistan on the International Monetary Fund's board, said he had come away reassured from a meeting with Prime Minister Nawaz Sharif in Lahore on Sunday.

"I was very encouraged by meeting (Sharif), who reiterated that the massive public mandate he was given provides him with the mandate to implement rapid, decisive policy measures to restore growth and increase employment in the economy," Mirakhor told the Lahore-based English-language daily The Nation published on Monday.

"The prime minister's priorities are the rapid reduction of inflation that has put a great burden on the masses, restore Pakistan's external credibility and creditworthiness, and strengthen confidence in the rupee," Mirakhor said.
The Finance Ministry said after the meeting that Pakistan's standby agreement remained on track and an IMF mission would visit Islamabad soon to review economic performance.
But in his first address to the nation since his landslide victory in February 3 elections, Sharif made no mention of the IMF and attacked his predecessors' reliance on foreign loans.
Pakistan must make payments of about $1.5 billion in February-June on its foreign debt of about $30 billion.
"Today the entire nation is looking towards us to break the shackles of foreign debt," he said, appealing to all Pakistanis to make donations, loans or deposits to help reduce the debt.

"Our donors order us around," Sharif said. "They pressure us to increase the electricity rates on an already poverty-ridden people. We are told to increase the price of flour, which is tantamount to snatching bread from our people."
Sharif announced a wage rise for junior civil servants and an increase in state pensions, without saying how these would be financed. He said power and telephone charges would be frozen.
He also pledged to enforce austerity and cut back public spending, except for defence, one of its main components.

Despite doubts about whether an elected government would stick to targets negotiated by its predecessors, the IMF resumed a standby loan in December after a caretaker government promised to cut the budget deficit to four percent of gross domestic product in 1996/97 (July-June) from 6.3 percent in 1995/96.
The IMF is likely to be concerned about any new measures likely to increase government spending, particularly in view of reports that revenue collection has fallen behind target.
Mirakhor said he would brief the IMF board in the second week of March. The IMF mission may arrive here by March 6.
The IMF is due to disburse the next $122 million tranche of the standby loan by March 31 if it is satisfied that Pakistan has met targets for the period up to the end of December.
Wary of Pakistan's track record of slippage, the fund is likely to ask hard questions of Sharif's economic team, which is yet to be announced, before endorsing its policy programme.
